title: UPGMA vs Neighbor-Joining, on a perfect matrix
summary: A matrix measured straight off a tree: Neighbor-Joining recovers it, UPGMA does not.

objectives: Compare Neighbor-Joining and UPGMA on the same distance matrix
Explain why UPGMA's clock assumption changes the tree it builds

source.citation: Constructed for NeoPhylo: the path-length matrix of a small non-clock-like teaching tree — every distance is the exact path between two tips of the reference tree

prompts.concept: The reference panel shows the true tree this matrix came from: every distance in the cells is the exact path between two tips of that tree. A matrix like this is called additive — it holds the whole tree, if the method can find it. Start with Neighbor-Joining: build and step to the end.
prompts.math: On an additive matrix, d(i,j) equals the total branch length on the path from i to j — building the tree is exactly the inverse problem of reading the matrix.

prompts.concept: If you are on Neighbor-Joining, the tree is now complete and the comparison shows no differences — every split of the true tree came back, because NJ is built to invert additive distances. Then switch the Method control to UPGMA and step through to the end: watch whether its tree still matches.
prompts.math: NJ's Q score corrects for how far each cluster sits from all the others, so it copes with branches of very different lengths.

prompts.concept: With UPGMA, the comparison shows a difference: UPGMA joins the closest pair and halves the distance — exact only when every tip is the same distance from the root. This tree is not clock-like, so its cluster averages pull a wrong pair together.
prompts.math: Cluster averaging keeps the matrix consistent only under a molecular clock; unequal branch lengths break it, and the wrong join order follows.
